My hon. friends titter.
The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) titters. Well, I say for his purpose and foi his enlightenment that I shall insert the words "Ontario and Quebec" where the act uses the word "provinces", and I do that in order to make it more clear and bring the matter concisely to our attention.
Whereas the provinces of Quebec, Ontario, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick have expresed their desire to he federally united into one dominion under the crown of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with a constitution similar in principle to that of the United Kingdom:
And whereas such a union would conduce to the welfare of the provinces and promote the interests of the British empire:
And so on. In other words, the very basis of the British North America Act is this: First, there is the principle of unity, the desire to unite together, and secondly united on the express desire of these four provinces. The provinces themselves initiated the movement to unite. They asked to be united, and they were united. They further expressed the view that such a union of these four provinces, and of course those which entered



Minimum Wage Draft Convention
later, would conduce to the welfare not of the dominion as a whole but to the welfare of the provinces.
Anything which conduces or is calculated to disunite this dominion must be considered to be at variance with the intention of the British North America Act. I ask parliament now to pause and consider this. What is there that is conducing or tending to disunite the provinces of Canada more than this inequality in provincial regulations covering matters common to the whole dominion? In this particular instance we refer to labour conditions. The labour conditions on the Pacific coast, in view of the minimum wage laws, are as my hon. friends know on a much higher basis, and higher rates are paid than obtain in Ontario, Quebec and elsewhere. The minimum wage law in Quebec is at variance with the minimum wage law in Ontario. I am not going into any comparison in an effort to indicate which is which, which is better, which is higher or which is lower, but I shall state briefly that they are at variance one with the other. With what result? In the first place we have this result, that there is a competition among manufacturers and industrial leaders to have their factories where they may obtain labour at the lowest cost. In the treaty of Versailles to which this parliament gave its adhesion, its support, its ratification there are words indicating that one of the things sought was to achieve a condition throughout the world whereby variations in social status, labour conditions, pay and so on would be brought into a more equitable and more even position.
Surely if we were sincere in our adherence to the treaty of Versailles, then we ought to do everything we can in this country to set our own house in order and to put our own affairs in harmony with the principle involved. It was indicated in the treaty of Versailles that one of the causes of war was the variation in social conditions of different countries. It is set forth in that treaty that it would be desirable so far as possible to remove such social variations, in order to prevent a recurrence of the great war. That is a most laudable object. If in Canada we are unwilling frankly to face conditions obtaining in this country, and if we are unwilling to set our country in order then I say we cannot claim to be very sincere in our adherence to the principles set forth in tha-t treaty.
I am sorry the hon. member for Quebec East is not in his seat, because I wish to direct a few observations to him. He made the statement that we were taking powers away from the provinces. I would not defy or
fMr. Stevens.]
challenge, but I would invite hon. member's of the legal profession in this chamber to show just where we are taking .powers from the provinces. If they wish to turn to the judgment of Lord Atkin, of the privy council, they will find his words as they were given in connection with the case P.A.T.A. v. Attorney General for Canada, appeal cases, 2 D.L.R. pages 11 and 12. I ask hon. members to follow these words because I believe they are peculiarly applicable and significant at this time.
If then the legislation-
The Combines Investigation Act-
-is authorized under one or the other of the heads specifically enumerated in section 91 it is not to the purpose to say that it affects property and civil rights in the provinces.
In other words, in the powers specifically set forth in section 91 there are powers at variance with the property and civil rights provision of section 92. Then it goes on:
Most of the specific subjects in section 91 do affect property and civil rights but so far as the legislation of parliament is operating within the enumerated' powers there is constitutional authority to interfere with property and civil rights.
In other words, no one can challenge the right of parliament as to any legislation that is included within the specific provisions of section 91 on the ground that it interferes with property and civil rights. I think that is clear and not disputed and the learned justice states that. But there are what are known as border-line matters which are not specifically provided for. Down through the years the tendency has been for the provinces to enlarge the powers granted under property and civil rights and to challenge the right of parliament if in the exercise of its general powers it is presumed to invade their interpretation of section 92.
An obligation rests upon parliament to give effect to a treaty into which it has entered and to legislate in the matter. There has been a tendency to disunite this country economically and socially through the vagaries of these laws and there is imposed upon parliament a fundamental and underlying duty to legislate in these matters unless they are specifically and directly excluded. I can see nothing in the British North America Act which specifically states that they shall not intervene in this matter.
We listened to a very learned if circuitous dissertation upon section 132. Even a high school student knows that this country was not exercising its treaty making powers in 1880 or thereabouts. While it does not state specifically the powers of Canada to-day it

Minimum Wage Draft Convention
cannot be said that the language is therefore faulty because we did not have treaty making powers in 1880. There does not seem to me to be any question but that it was intended by the British North America Act that where Canada had entered into obligations with the peoples of the world or other parts of the empire, then the Canadian parliament must exercise its powers to give effect to the obligations so entered into.
I am not a lawyer but I remember reading a very learned argument by Alexander Hamilton. It would repay any Canadian to read these arguments of Alexander Hamilton. He was trying to work out and did work out for President Washington some very remarkable laws which he brought within the constitution of the United States. There was one principle which he fastened upon, and I should like to outline this to the house. I look upon Alexander Hamilton as being one of the greatest Americans, not only of his time but of all times. He said that where the constitution gave congress certain power as a federal body it was implied that congress had the right to enact laws which were necessary in order to carry that power into effect. I have not given the beautiful and chaste language which Alexander Hamilton used, but any hon. member who is interested can get this from the library. This was his argument in support of the establishment of a state bank in the United States. It was argued that congress had not the right to create a corporation, that that right rested with the states. Alexander Hamilton said: You have the right to control finance, you have the right to issue money and there is an implied right to erect a corporation to give effect to these matters. He argued that the federal authorities had that right, and the law was passed. That argument has been the foundation in a large measure of much of the interpretation of the constitution of the United States, and it is very apt and applicable to the Canadian situation to-day.
If the Canadian parliament is entrusted with the power to preserve unity or, as was stated a moment ago, peace, order and good government; if it is to give effect to international obligations, which it must do if it is to be an entity; if parliament is clothed with that responsibility then surely it must claim the right to pass the necessary legislation. My chief complaint in regard to this measure is that it was not ratified before. Perhaps I can claim exemption from blame in this respect, because in 1920 I seconded a resolution which was moved in this house asking for the ratification of labour matters. It is interesting 92582-llli
to read the opinion of the late Mr. Doherty, who was then Minister of Justice. He spoke against the resolution which Mr. Burnham introduced and which I seconded yet I have in my hand a copy of some of his statements which shows that in his opinion power rested in this parliament under section 132 to do those things which were then asked to be done and which were similar to what is now being asked. I think this convention which was passed in 1928 should have been ratified long ago.
I say to my colleagues in this house that one of the causes of the problems facing parliament to-day is the fact that parliament has failed to occupy the field properly given to it by the British North America Act. I shall give a very striking illustration of this. Under subsection 2 of section 91 there is a very specific power granted. This section reads:
It shall be lawful for the Queen, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons, to make laws for the peace, order, and good government of Canada, in relation to all matters not coming within the classes of subjects by this act assigned exclusively to the legislatures of the provinces; and for greater certainty, but not so as to restrict the generality of the foregoing terms of this section, it is hereby declared that (notwithstanding anything in this act) the exclusive legislative authority of the parliament of Canada extends to all matters coming within the classes of subjects next hereinafter enumerated, that is to say,

2. The regulation of trade and commerce.
I know that legal gentlemen will say: Oh, that is all right but the courts have given decisions on this and that. I say to them and I say to parliament that that is one of the reasons why we are embarrassed to-day. We have had these adverse court decisions and parliament has never seriously attempted to occupy the field which is included in the term " the regulation of trade and commerce." We have tacitly left the domestic field to the provinces; we have interpreted that as meaning that we should deal only with extraterritorial or international trade and as a result there has grown up in this country the belief that we have not the power. We have failed to occupy the field, and there is in economics an old doctrine that if a field of activity is not occupied by one party and another party does occupy it, that party gets a vested right in the field. And so the provinces to-day-and I am not quarrelling with them for it-are claiming rights under property and civil rights, which properly come under section 91, subsection 2. Had this parliament, twenty, thirty, forty or fifty years ago set itself to the task of reasonable regulation of trade within Canada there would be no
1750	COMMONS
Minimum Wage Draft Convention
challenge of its rights at the present time. But it has never attempted to do so. It has kept away from it, and now we are faced with these adverse decisions and objections and arguments. I submit that in this matter of the regulation of trade and commerce within Canada, on this question of the social and industrial relations of the citizens of Canada, this parliament has a duty to perform; and instead of debating as we did in the early part of this session, day after day, technical matters with hairsplitting legal arguments pro and con-and to-day we have had two learned speeches from hon. gentlemen in this house, who gave this view or that view-instead of having such arguments, I say, if we could only enlist for one session of parliament the cooperation of the legal gentlemen of this house in trying to work out these matters, we could make some progress and have a successful issue of many of these problems.
I do not for one moment suggest that we should disregard provincial rights. I think that in the past there has been too great a tendency to approach these questions in an attitude of exclusiveness-the attitude that we have certain rights which we are going to exercise, and that we shall disregard the provinces. These provinces, all of them, are administered by human beings like ourselves; and I believe that if an approach were made to the provinces in a proper attitude, in a friendly spirit, in a conciliatory manner-and I know that some of them do recognize that this is a problem that must be faced and dealt with-I say that if we approached the provinces in a spirit of cooperation, with a desire to solve these problems in a spirit of harmony, we should make progress. That, sir, I think is important.
My hon. friend from Quebec East referred to the delegates to the conference of the league. He said that if we pass this legislation there will be a tendency in the future for delegates to the labour convention under the League of Nations to arrogate to themselves the right to vary or amend the constitution. I do not think there is any danger of that. I know that most of those who have been to the labour convention since it was inaugurated, representatives appointed by the right hon. gentleman opposite and representatives appointed on this side, are serious-minded, earnest, honest and reputable citizens of Canada, and I cannot conceive of any delegation such as would be appointed by a responsible government of Canada doing anything of that kind. They do come before us or present through the government the findings of the international labour convention.
! Mr St evens. 1
That is what they go there for; that is what they are sent there for. The international labour convention weighs these problems, studies them and comes to certain decisions. Will anyone question the soundness and advisability of the decisions regarding, for instance, international trade in narcotics? A great deal of good has been done in that respect. I fancy that the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Matthews), if he were speaking now, would tell the house that much valuable assistance has been given the officers of his department in dealing with this very perplexing problem, one of the most human of all problems. And this arose out of the labour convention. There are other matters of similar importance. This one is peculiarly appropriate at the moment. Here we are faced with this problem in Canada-the vagaries and differences that exist; and surely it is our duty, if we can possibly do so, to harmonize these differences in Canada so as to bring about an understanding one with the other so far as the provinces are concerned. Let this parliament, as the constitutional body to do it, take the lead and assume the responsibility, and in due process of performing its duty bring about a better condition and at the same time discharge a wry solemn obligation which we undertook at the time of the signing of the treaty of Versailles.
The hon. member for Quebec East referred to another matter. He spoke in rather emphatic language, with a warning to my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) about soap box oratory and a few other things, and he said that the constitution is our safeguard. Of course it is. The inference from that language is that anyone who takes a view such as I now take is playing with the constitution, disregarding the sanctity of the constitution. I am just as jealous of the constitution of Canada as the hon. gentleman is, but no harm will ever be done the constitution by a frank discussion in this house, or by searching through it for powers in order to give effect to legislation which we think is good for the people of Canada. There ought to be a little more of the positive and a little less of narrow legal interpretation of the constitution, a little more effort to find within the confines of the constitution the power to do those things that will be in the interests of the people of the country as a whole, instead of throwing legal obstacles in the way. And the time for such an effort is now.

Minimum Wage Draft Convention
We still have a million and a quarter or more of people on relief. I am not saying that as a reflection on anybody; the refleet-tion is upon us all. But there are a million and a quarter people on relief, and this is one of the measures, one and only one, and I might say one of the minor measures, that might be adopted towards the solution of that problem. Surely therefore it is time the house addressed itself in a positive spirit towards these things rather than in a negative spirit of legal interpretation-I endorse the phrase of an hon. member over here, and I say that we should have a human interpretation of these matters.
I am not going to detain the house at greater length, though there is much more that I might say. I wish, however, to refer to one thing more. The hon. gentleman said among other things that the house was being deceived, that when the treaty of Versailles was passed the house was told that any measures that were brought forward under No. 405 of the treaty would be subject to the proper constitutional body in the country, and he said that that was particularly provided for Canada and other federally organized states. And I think the Secretary of State repeated that. The inference was that by bringing this measure in, the house was being deceived. Well, in September, 1919, Sir Robert Borden, who represented this country as the senior delegate from Canada, and as Prime Minister of the country, returned from the deliberations with regard to the treaty and gave the dominion certain views in an official way. From these observations I will quote very briefly:
Side by side with the covenant-[DOT]

I would have taken the trouble to get the original, only I did not think it was necessary to do so. Sir Robert Borden said:
Side by side with the covenant stand the provisions of the labour convention.
I just pause there. Side by side with the covenant of the League of Nations, of the treaty of Versailles, stand the provisions of the labour convention. That was the first
intimation this house had of the attitude of the dominion government of that day-and parliament accepted that attitude-of the relation of these labour conventions to the treaty of Versailles, and what this house might expect in its attitude and obligation toward them. Sir Robert Borden continued:
It was my privilege to attend the earlier meetings of the commission which framed the articles on that subject now embodied in part XIII of the treaty. At one of these meetings the preamble of the labour convention was framed. It is as follows:
And whereas conditions of labour exist involving such injustice, hardship and privation to large numbers of people as to produce unrest so great that the peace and harmony of the world are imperilled; an improvement of those conditions is urgently required; as, for example, by the regulation of the hours of work.
Whereas also the failure of any nation to adopt humane conditions of labour is an obstacle in the way of other nations which desire to improve the conditions in their own countries. . . .
Holding as they do, that labour should not be regarded merely as an article of commerce, they think that there are methods and principles for regulating labour conditions which all industrial communities should endeavour to apply so far as their special circumstances will permit.
This language was given to this house by Sir Robert Borden when he returned from the drafting and the passing of the treaty of Versailles, and I invite the house again to listen to these words:
Conditions of labour exist involving such injustice, hardship and privation to large numbers of people as to produce unrest so great that the peace and harmony of the world are imperilled.
I say that the conditions, the sense of injustice, of inequity of things and the hardship and privation suffered by workers today in Canada as well as elsewhere-and one has but to turn one's eyes to the United States to see this condition in perhaps its worst form-are, taking them from a worldwide standpoint, quite as serious to-day as they were when these words were penned and when they were submitted to the house.
An improvement of those conditions is urgently required-
No one will doubt that. Those were the words given to the house when this treaty was first brought here in 1919.
-as for example, by the regulation of the hours of work.
And so forth. So I conclude with this, that in my opinion the house should support the government in passing this legislation. We have the assurance of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie), for which I again thank him, that the government not only intends

Mr. Speaker, if anything were needed to make it perfectly clear that the position which the opposition have taken with respect to the government's so-called social legislation is the correct one, namely, that it would have -been advisable to obtain -in th-e first instance an opinion from the Supreme Court of Canada as to whether it is within the competence of this parliament to enact the various measures of social legislation that are being brought down, it would be found in what we have witnessed in this house this afternoon. I have no desire to enter upon another long discussion of the constitutional aspects of the question. The debate, to which we have listened this afternoon, has, in that particular, been largely a repetition of arguments that have been presented before. It is true that, in what both the cx-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) and the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) have said, we have had important and very valuable additions in the way of opinion with respect to points that will come up in controversy. But of one thing there can be no uncertainty whatever, and that is that so far as the question of the competence- of this parliament is concerned in presenting for enactment measures of this kind, with any hope of their enforcement, there is the gravest possible doubt.
I much less wish to enter into what appears to be an irreconcilable -family quarrel among hon. gentlemen opposite; but I think I should point out that what there has been of controversy, of difference of opinion, in the house this afternoon, has not for the most part been between those of us who sit, sir, to your left as an opposition and hon gentlemen who sit to your right as the government and its supporters, but that the sharpest and most acrimonious differences of opinion we have witnessed in parliament this year have been among hon. gentlemen opposite. What we have been, I shall not say privileged but, forced to witness is in the nature of what evidently has taken place in the cabinet when these very measures have been under consideration. It is quite apparent from what
[Mr Stevens.]
the hon. member who has just taken his seat, the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), has said, there was a very serious difference of opinion between the ministers of the crown when these matters were under discussion, and that he held one view and that some of his colleagues held another. In that regard, just in passing, may I draw attention to the fact that the hon. member addressed his question as to the competence of parliament to enact this legislation and what was intended to be done about- enforcing it, to the acting leader of the government (Sir George Perley), but he was replied to not by the acting leader but by the Minister of Justice. That is a significant fact, one to which attention should certainly be drawn. It is quite apparent t-h-at however the forces have been divided, they have been divided in a very real way. Indeed one has only to look at the correspondence which passed between the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and the ex-Minister o-f Trade and Commerce at the time my hon. friend's resignation was accepted to see that the Prime Minister told him then in no uncertain language that he was putting forward in the cabinet at that time views which could not be entertained by his colleagues, that he was raising with respect to legislation hopes in the minds of the people of the country which there was no justification for raising, and that he was at fault in so doing. If that has been the kind of thing that has been going on in the cabinet with respect to this social legislation, is it any wonder that after hon. gentlemen opposite have had some six months in which to try to reconcile their differences, we on this side, when all this social legislation is suddenly brought before us, should feel that at least there is need for a little more in the way of careful consideration of the authority of parliament before proceeding too far with these enactments.
May I ask this question: is it going to help to bring about the great objective which my hon. friend who has just taken his seat says he has in view, which members of the present government say they have in view, that the country now knows that in this parliament itself there is difference of opinion not only between hon. gentlemen who sit to the right and those who sit to the left of Mr. Speaker, but a cleavage in the ranks of the government itself and its supporters? There could be no more obvious evidence of the uncertainty of the whole situation. The government has proceeded to build its house on the sands of controversy and dissension, instead of seeking to construct it

Minimum Wage Draft Convention
upon the rock of constitutional authority, right and power, which admits of no uncertainty.
May I also say to my hon. friend that when he speaks about parliament itself deciding what it shall do in these matters, and taking upon itself not merely to enact legislation but also to interpret it; when he speaks about viewing the constitution as something which is sacred and therefore to be regarded with a degree of reverence, it must be remembered that under the constitution this parliament is only one branch of government. There are three branches of government under the constitution, each of which has a distinctive and known jurisdiction and obligation. Parliament is the legislative branch; it enacts the laws. There is the executive branch for the carrying out of the laws, and, there is also the judicial branch for the interpretation of the laws. We in this parliament may discuss the matter from now until doomsday, but we cannot give to any law enacted here, and make it hold, an interpretation other than that which the courts will finally place upon it. That is known.
I shall not say what I think must have been in the mind of my hon. friend when he tried to indicate that the ex-Minister of Justice, the hon. member for Quebec East was more concerned with the legal view of things than with the humane view. In so saying, he was simply playing to the gallery, he was simply indulging in claptrap.

subtopic: APPROVAL OF DRAFT CONVENTION ADOPTED BY GENERAL CONFERENCE, INTERNATIONAL LABOUR ORGANIZATION
speechtext:
I am not
going to repeat what I have said previously. I think the record of the Liberal party in the matter of labour legislation is well enough known in this country not to require special emphasis now; its record in the enactment of social measures and the nature and extent of them are very generally known. But I
1754	COMMONS
Minimum Wage Draft Convention
ask my hon. friends: What about the past five years? Every time they seek to stress the argument that these measures should have been enacted nine years ago, they doubly condemn themselves for not having enacted them within the last five years. Some of these things were not possible years ago, as they are to-day and have been since 1930. Times change, conditions change, new problems come to the fore. W'hen the last Liberal government was in office it was dealing with post-war problems and the condition of the country as it had resulted from the war, questions that to the exclusion of others had to be dealt with immediately. This is an age in which social problems are being dealt with in all quarters of the globe, and it is natural they should come up in this parliament at this time. We on this side from 1930 until this present year, over and over again directed attention of hon. gentlemen opposite to the fact that then was the time for them to bring about a conference between the provinces and the dominion with a view to settling the question of the legislative competence and authority of parliament on matters of social legislation; that during this parliament was the time to bring about a conference which would obtain the agreement of the provinces to many of these measures, and above all the time in which, if the British North America Act required amendment as we say we believe it does, that amendment should be brought about. But that step has not been taken, and the result is that to-day we are exactly where it was indicated five years ago parliament would find itself, unless some immediate step were taken to have the British North America Act amended and authority given parliament to enact measures of this kind.
When there is mention of the desirability of uniformity of minimum industrial standards there is as I see it no division of view among hon. members of this house. We may have individual differences as to the particular point at which a given standard should be placed, but generally speaking I think everyone in this parliament holds the view that uniformity of labour standards, constituting a national minimum, is a desirable thing, not only within one country but, if it can be obtained, throughout the world. Indeed, that is the whole objective of the labour office and conference of the League of Nations. We are all united as to the desirability of uniformity in minimum standards. The whole question of difference between us is the question of method. Until this year we have always assumed that the provinces .were the bodies
(Mr. Mackenzie King.]
that had the legislative competence to pass minimum wage laws, eight hour day legislation and other measures of the kind. If we were not of that opinion, and if the provinces were not of that opinion, how is the fact to be accounted for that all the provinces of Canada have enacted legislation of that very kind? The very fact that you have the provincial statutes filled with social legislation is evidence of the fact that the provinces have regarded that subject as coming within their particular sphere. But as they have legislated, it has become obvious that there are differences in the laws of the different provinces. I am not so sure that some of those differences have not arisen out of the differences in economic development and the resources and the nature of the industries in the different provinces. In great industrial provinces like Ontario and Quebec the situation is bound to be different from the situation in the prairie provinces, and conditions in the maritimes and on the prairies are bound to be different from conditions in British Columbia. As time goes on industrial standards will come more and more to find the one level, but I submit that you are not going to bring about the level that is desired by adopting in this parliament a course which is arbitrary and unconstitutional, when all the while there is before you an obviously right and simple course to follow. What we on this side have been contending for is the course that we believe in the end will be the surest, safest and swiftest course in bringing about uniformity of legislation. The provinces can be brought together in agreement not only with themselves but also with the federal government on these matters. The social conscience is awakened at this time as never before, and there will be a desire, I am sure, in any great conference of the provinces and the dominion properly constituted and conducted to harmonize the views of all parties on these questions of minimum standards in industry. Our view all along has been that this was the step that ought to be taken first.
I believe there will be found agreement between the provinces and the dominion as to the desirability of amending the British North America Act first of all, so as to give to ourselves the power to amend our own constitution and to this parliament the right to legislate on certain of these matters of social legislation to be very clearly defined. But when that question is being fully discussed, I believe it will be found to be inseparable from the whole question of the financial relations between the dominion and the provinces. I believe that what will be as necessary as

Minimum Wage Draft Convention
agreement between the provinces and the dominion in matters affecting the amendment of the British North America Act will be very careful consideration of the financial relations between the provinces and the dominion, which will result in the dominion assuming some of the obligations that to-day belong to the provinces or giving to the provinces certain rights with respect to sources of revenue which at the moment	they may not
have. I believe the two subjects will be found to be interrelated and intertwined; but I do also submit that we will not hasten the day, and we will not make the situation any more secure, by taking a step in this parliament which, instead of seeking to bring the provinces and the dominion into closer relationship, is raising a question of difference between them.
That brings to mind what my hon. friend has just said about unity in Canada. One of the strong objections, I think, to the manner in which the government is proceeding with this legislation is that it is tending to divide this country instead of to unite it; it is tending to emphasize differences between the provinces and the dominion. Indeed, the whole underlying danger of the situation is that, as the result of political discussion during a general election, it may raise all kinds of controversy in connection with provincial rights versus dominion rights. Well, if we have that sort of thing added to all the uncertainty that exists in the country, and in the world to-day, I am afraid we are going to be much further away from national unity at the end of a political campaign, whatever may be its results, than we have been at any time heretofore.
Once more, in view of what we have heard this afternoon from the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan), who gave us the benefit of his wide knowledge and experience with regard to these questions of constitutional obligation and law, and from the ex-Minister of Trade and Commerce, who gave us the difference of view that existed in the government and what he put forth as the point of view he thought should be made to prevail, I would hope that even yet the government might see the wisdom, while in no way ceasing to go on with the enactment of these measures, of referring one or more of them to the supreme court for an opinion before an endeavour is made to put them all into force in this country. I do not say that with any desire to impede the enactment of these measures, or their operation subsequently, but I do say that if you have an eight hour day law put into force, immediately some injunction will be issued against
the enforcement of some essential provision, the case will be tested in the courts and the effective operation of the legislation will be held up. Then if an adverse decision is given, immediately you will have another test case with regard to the minimum wage legislation, and the same thing will happen in regard to these other pieces of social legislation that have been introduced. The result will be that neither labour nor capital, neither the employer, the employee or the public, neither the business man, the merchant nor anyone else will know where he stands or where he is likely to be with regard to the laws of the country. That is a very dangerous position in which to put a country when conditions are as serious as they are in the world at the present time. That can be avoided if hon. gentlemen will take the one step I have all along been urging; and may I point out that they have made the way very easy for themselves. As we were told by the Minister of Labour (Mr. jGordon) yesterday, he is allowing three months before his eight hour day bill goes into effect. The Prime Minister has told us that it will be some considerable time before an attempt will be made to assess any dues under the unemployment insurance act, and that all that will be attempted in the first instance is the creation of the commission. I have no doubt at all that we shall find the same amendment, as to delay in enforcement, placed in this act with regard to minimum wages, allowing another three months or so to elapse before it will come into operation. Then there is the amendment in regard to the day of rest, which means another three months or so in that case. Within that period of time any one or all of these measures could be referred by the government to the supreme court and an opinion obtained, just as was done with respect to the other measures mentioned this afternoon by the ex-Minister of Justice. If the court says the enactment of these measures is within the competence of parliament, then I think everyone will be tremendously relieved and will do the best he can to see that the decision given is upheld. If however the step suggested is not taken, I venture to say we will find the validity of every one of these acts contested in the courts. The controversy will run from the local courts to the supreme court, and from the supreme court to the judicial committee of the privy council. A year or two hence, we will probably find ourselves in the position where all the government's social legislation has been upset, with the result that the whole business of legislation will have to be begun de novo.

Minimum Wage Draft Convention
I believe what we have witnessed this afternoon is quite sufficient to justify every word I have said by way of observation upon rather than of criticism of the remarks of hon. members opposite, and certainly is sufficient to justify the attitude the official opposition has taken from the beginning with regard to all this social legislation.

Mr. Speaker, l'Ulustra-tion of to-day's date contains the following article:
To-day, the house established three records: this afternoon, for speed; this evening, for weakness and imbecility. The weakness, alas, was that of Hon. Arthur Sauve, whose estimates were voted. The imbeciles were those who, for two whole hours by the clock, with incredible meanness, vented criticism and attacks on the Postmaster General. The Attack
In justice to Mr. Pouliot, let us say that, while his attacks were the most violent of those showered on Mr. Sauve, they were the most intelligent, the most methodical and, therefore, the most formidable.
To write that an imbecile made the most intelligent attack, one must have reached the depths of stupidity. That such a person should use the word "imbecile," I care very little; but when he adds that an imbecile made the most intelligent attack, he perpetrates a grave insult.
If I catch him at it again, I will amuse the house with the strange tale of the knife and the no less strange one of the Nelson column.

On the orders of the day:
Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING
(Leader of the Opposition): Mr. Speaker, apparently my hon. friend the Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) is leading the house at the moment. I rather hesitate to ask him the question I have in mind. However, I think I
should have it immediately of record. The other day I asked the acting Prime Minister (Sir George Perley) if he could give the house some information as to when we might expect the report of the royal commission on price spreads and mass buying. In this evening's Ottawa Journal I notice an article which no doubt appears in other evening papers. This article is headed:	-
Stevens' Program on Price Spreads Presented.
Abolish Rebates Exceeding Total of Five Per Cent.
Suggests Application of Dumping Duties in Domestic Trade to Overcome Special Prices to Mass Buyers.
Would tax Salaries Over $10,000 and Regulate Set-up of Firms.
Hon. H. H. Stevens, former Minister of Trade and Commerce, has presented his recommendations to the price spreads commission to establish fair and just practices in the marketing and distribution system of Canada.
I should like to know whether the government regards this commission as a judicial body or whether it is a publicity bureau. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when this
bill was receiving its second reading I indicated that I had some statements to make with regard to certain conditions which had arisen under the operation of the old treaty, and the minister in charge of the bill indicated that it would be acceptable for me to make these statements at this stage of the bill.
I think it is generally agreed that if we are to recover world trade and eliminate restrictions on trade, it can be done only by way of treaties such as this. These treaties should be devised to facilitate trade rather than to act as restrictions, as certain of them seem to have done. It may be that the minister will be able to give a satisfactory explanation of certain conditions which have arisen. These treaties are supposed to confer a benefit upon Canada in two different ways: first, by allowing a greater volume of exports to the country with which we have made a treaty, and, second, by permitting the receiving of goods from that country at a lower rate of duty, thus conferring a benefit upon the people. There would seem to be some indications that the French treaty is not satisfactory from the latter point of view.
I have in my hand a letter which was addressed to Mr. McGregor, registrar of the Combines Investigation Act, by a firm styling themselves Drug Agencies. It would seem that before this treaty came into effect this particular firm was buying certain pharmaceutical preparations in the open market in France. They claim that they are now unable to do this because of article 9 of the French treaty, which reads:
Either of the high contracting parties may require that goods imported into its territory and coming from the territory of the other, shall be accompanied by a certificate of origin delivered in conformity with the laws of the country of origin; provided, however, that a presentation of the certificate of origin shall be obligatory in the case of importation of pharmaceutical specialties, toilet articles and articles of perfumery. Such certificate shall be issued or delivered by the competent authority in the country of origin and shall be visaed by the consular or other authority of the country of destination.
I had on the order paper a question which I withdrew asking whether both parties to the treaty were insisting upon certificates of origin. At that time I had not read this article, and it seems that it was optional with either country to ask for the certificate of origin except with respect to pharmaceutical preparations. Now the complaint is made by those who have brought the matter to my

attention that this particular article was introduced into the treaty at the request of the Canadian government. Of course the fact that it is here indicates that both parties have agreed to it. But I cannot understand why special emphasis should be laid on pharmaceutical preparations unless for the reason suggested by those who are making the complaint, namely, that the Canadian government wished to give to certain interests a monopoly of the importation of these preparations. It appears that certificates of origin are granted in France by the chamber of commerce; that is the body that has been delegated to give these certificates, and I understand that they will give them only to the manufacturers of these preparations. The result is, as complained, that they can no longer be bought in the open market and that certain interests in Canada have .therefore a monopoly in the handling of these preparations. It is claimed that about seven hundred different articles come within this category. I know that the argument is advanced that it is necessary to have the certificate of origin in older to protect our own country against importations from other countries via France. On the other hand it might be supposed that the French government would require these certificates of origin in order that France might have all the benefits of the treaty to which she is entitled. But in actual practice the price of these pharmaceutical preparations has been increased by reason of the situation that prevails.
I listened with interest to the explanation which the minister gave yesterday to the hon. member for Bonaventure with respect to the price of wines and liquors, in which he indicated that the depreciation of the Canadian currency was responsible in large measure for the increase in price. It is quite possible that this may be one factor in this particular problem, but it would be interesting to know whether the fact that under the operation of the treaty as it now exists the particular firms interested have a monopoly in the handling of these preparations is not also a factor in the increased price, because it seems to be generally admitted that the price of these preparations has been increased.
The statement is made in a letter which I have here that under the French treaty these same interests now handling these preparations made an application to the former government to have a clause similar to article 9 of the treaty inserted, but it was refused at that time. If any light can be thrown on the subject we shall be pleased to have it, because it does seem that the consumers of these preparations are not getting the benefit which we should

Canada-France Agreement
expect they would be entitled to under a lower rate of duty as provided for in the treaty; and if the effect has been, as it would seem to be, to restrict the trade to a few individuals instead of throwing it open to the general public who might wish to buy goods in the open market in France, then it would appear that the treaty is not working out as we should like.
Another instance has come to my attention, and though it may not have so direct a bearing on the French treaty, nevertheless it is connected with our trade with France. The complaint is made that importations of beeswax are coming from England under the preferential rates and that a large part of these importations comes from France and the French colonies. According to certain statistics received by the British trade commissioner in Montreal in April, 1934, it appears that Great Britain receives two-thirds of its imports from France and French colonies. The man who makes the complaint says that he is now no longer able to buy beeswax direct from France because of the higher rate of duty. I find, on looking over the treaty, that this article is not mentioned. At any rate, this man complains that he can no longer obtain beeswax direct from France and that Great Britain is being given an unfair advantage under the agreement with her, since a good deal of what she ships to us is imported from other countries. Personally I am not very much exercised as a rule over the fact that we are getting quantities of goods at a lower rate of duty, but if there is no reduction in the price and our revenue is suffering at the same time, this may be a matter to be looked into. Perhaps the minister has some explanation to give in regard to some of the statements I have made.

speechtext:
The hon. gentleman gave
me no notice of his inquiry wuth regard to beeswax. My memory is not sufficiently accurate to say whether beeswax was one of the products from France brought in under the preferential duty. If I remember rightly it is not included, and if beeswax is not included in the Canada-France treaty I do not quite see how the government of this country can make arrangements for the merchant, whom my hon. friend is representing to-night, to purchase in France what the French merchants are not willing to sell to him. Possibly they send their large supply to Great Britain, and it is distributed from there throughout the other parts of the world.

maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE TRADE AGREEMENT   BILL TO CONFIRM ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL OF 1935 TO THE CONVENTION OF 1933
speechtext: The complaint is with regard to the higher duty coming from France

maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE TRADE AGREEMENT   BILL TO CONFIRM ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL OF 1935 TO THE CONVENTION OF 1933
speechtext:
If a man buys directly in
France and brings the article in here from that country, then it comes under the terms of the French treaty, and if that beeswax is not on the intermediate tariff or the intermediate tariff less a discount, he cannot bring it in under a lower rate of duty from France. He therefore finds it to his advantage undoubtedly to buy in the English market and to bring it in from there. As to whether all the beeswax bought in England is produced in England, I cannot give my hon. friend definite information. If it is a matter of sufficient importance into which the Department of Trade and Commerce might inquire as to whether any prejudice is thereby effected to the Canadian importer of beeswax, I cannot say definitely.
On the other question as to article 9, it is obvious that in any trade treaty between Canada and France in which preferential rates are given in Canada on the one hand to French products and in France on the other hand to Canadian products, there must be some way devised by which when goods are imported into this country it may be ascertained that the products are really French, and that products going from Canada to France are Canadian. Therefore, as usual in such treaties, provision is made with regard to giving certificates of origin. In this connection article 9 states:
Such certificate shall be issued or delivered by the competent authority in the country of origin and shall be visaed by the consular or other authority in the country of destination.
We have not in this country any governmental authority which is authorized to give certificates with regard to products exported to France, and therefore the French have agreed to take certificates from those who produce these products in Canada, provided that the certificate so given by the producer in this country is visaed by the consular officer of France in Canada. Therefore if there is a sale of lobster's or salmon from British Columbia to a French importer, those who conduct the trade in Vancouver for instance, give certificates, which are then verified by affidavit or statutory declaration usually, and those together with the export documents are visaed by a French consular officer. On the production of those certificates and the French visa at the French port of importation, the products are passed by the French officials. On the other hand goods imported into Canada from France are accompanied by a certificate of origin. This
Canada-France Agreement

certificate is given in France under the authority of the French government, an authority which has been delegated to the chambre de commerce which is extremely desirous of ascertaining that the goods so exported are really French products. In connection with this article 9, a special clause is inserted:
Provided, however, that the presentation of a certificate of origin shall be obligatory in the ease of importation of pharmaceutical specialties, toilet articles and articles of perfumery.
France depends to a very considerable extent upon her exports of these specialties. Her pharmaceutical specialties are produced under government supervision and the perfumery production of France is very large and is exported to almost all foreign countries. I know, in visiting the ports of South America or 'Central America or Mexico, that one will find such French articles are on sale in those countries to the extent of constituting almost a monopoly. The French government therefore insisted upon the inclusion of this proviso in article 9, upon the ground that they wished to prevent misrepresentation in regard to pharmaceutical specialties, toilet articles and articles of perfumery which did not come up to their standard, and which when they went abroad ruined the reputation of the French production in those articles, which reputation it had taken years and very considerable expense to establish in the consuming countries of the world. Therefore, to prevent what I might call boot-legging in connection with those articles, to prevent false representations being made in foreign markets with regard to them, the French government insisted that there should be certificates of origin produced from the French authority as to the French origin of those articles in order that there might be no misrepresentation in the consuming country. That proviso I can assure the hon. gentleman was introduced at the request of the French government. In respect of importations into Canada from France of pharmaceutical specialties, toilet articles and articles of perfumery, the French government insisted upon a certificate l>emg given to the French manufacturers or producers that those articles which are exported to Canada under the preferential rates are manufactured or produced in France. Perhaps those who have made representations to the hon. gentleman are more interested in the illicit trade which exists in France and every other country in pharmaceutical specialties, articles of perfumery and so forth rather than in the purchase of the standard articles concerning which the French government has
[Mr. Cahan.j
exercised such great care. However the decision of the customs branch of the Department of National Revenue has been that perfumeries, ' whether produced in Italy or Switzerland or Belgium or some other country, if they have been bootlegged into France, cannot come into Canada as French products unless a certificate of origin is given as provided in article 9. That is all the explanation I can give to the hon. gentleman.

maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE TRADE AGREEMENT   BILL TO CONFIRM ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL OF 1935 TO THE CONVENTION OF 1933
speechtext:
I do not just follow the
minister's logic. If the preservation of the purity of these articles was as important to the French government as he indicates, they would see that no certificates of origin were given except to those who exported the standard article. There would be no necessity for putting it in the treaty; we would have expected them to attend to it on their own account. The fact that special emphasis has been laid upon it in the treaty raises the suspicion that it was inserted at the request not of the French government but of the Canadian government to protect certain monopolistic industries.

maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE TRADE AGREEMENT   BILL TO CONFIRM ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL OF 1935 TO THE CONVENTION OF 1933
speechtext:
I can only say that was the
reason given, that they wished to preserve not only the purity of their products ooming within these special classes but also to preserve the reputation of their products in foreign countries, because throughout the world France has a reputation for those articles. Whether the French government could have found other means of preventing the illicit sale of pharmaceutical articles which are not manufactured under government supervision I cannot say, because I have nothing to do with the administration of French affairs. But one thing is sure, that the means which they did take of insisting on the insertion of this proviso in article 9 have apparently been very effective in preventing the export from France to Canada of low standard products of these three classes, of which the French government does not approve.

maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE TRADE AGREEMENT   BILL TO CONFIRM ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL OF 1935 TO THE CONVENTION OF 1933
speechtext:
Would the minister teH
us when this article 9 first appeared? Was that clause not in the old treaty? Article 9 is in the 1922 treaty. You will recall, Mr. Chairman, as you were in the house at the time this treaty with France was first introduced by the present opposition, that I took a very decided stand against the treaty from beginning to end. This treaty is not improved a great deal. I will admit that there are some improvements, but not many. The old treaty was cluttered up with lists

Canada-France Agreement
of two hundred articles specially mentioned as articles that we could ship to France but we never have made one of them. I object to some of the clauses in this treaty as much as I ever did. It has not been changed; the old treaty remains the same; these are additions to it, and I am not going to sit here and allow it to pass without making a protest. The minimum clause still remains, and that works a hardship on us. We made that treaty in good faith, and when we made it the minimum clause was there and our wheat went to France subject to a duty of ten cents a bushel. Under the treaty they had the right to raise that minimum tariff to anything they saw fit, and before long it was put up to a dollar, which was prohibitive. I say that a treaty made on that basis is wrong.
There is another feature. The goods that we take under this new protocol from France consist of what? Take a glance at them. They start with Rocquefort cheese and Camemlbert cheese. The next item is pepper, to which I have no objection because I think it is needed for certain purposes. Then we have canned mushrooms, candied chestnuts, liqueurs, cognac brandy and Armagnaic brandy. Fine. Now let us take a look at the list of stuff that we can take from France. Mind you, the duty on these articles is reduced very materially. Let us see what they are and whether the constituents of the hon. member for Lisgar are going to be much affected by them. Lace and embroideries, wholly of cotton; fibres of raffia or of sisal; lace and embroideries, wholly of flax, or of hemp, or of flax, hemp and cotton; women's dress gloves of kid, elbow length. For the life of me I cannot understand how it is that on luxuries on which we should collect the duty is reduced. Of course the hon. member for Lisgar is glad to see a reduction of duty, provided the reduction gets to his people. But imagine his people buying that class of goods! They work so hard they are not using any embroideries just now. My contention is that articles of this kind should pay duty and pay it through the nose; people using articles of this kind should pay for them. In my judgment the minimum tariff is an improper basis on which to make any treaty with any country. We can do without their trade if we cannot trade on better terms than that. If we wanted to change the tariff we could not do it unless we got their permission, but they could change it to our disadvantage. The only way that we could alter anything was by abrogating the treaty, which we were forced to do. Just think of that.
There are some other things I object to in this treaty as affecting my constituents. I would ask the minister how it comes that such a great reduction is made on cheap wines. My county is interested in wine manufacture. There is not a farmer in my district who has not a vineyard; in that district thirty thousand tons of grapes are grown in a year, and half of them are pressed into wine. I know one plant that pressed eight thousand tons of grapes. My people in three counties are dependent upon that; it is the best crop they have. I should like to know why a reduction of fifty per cent is made in the duty on French wines. Are we encouraging the growing of grapes in France? Is that the proposition? Not for me. I am encouraging the growing of grapes at home; that is what I am interested in, and that is why I am speaking on the subject.

maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE TRADE AGREEMENT   BILL TO CONFIRM ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL OF 1935 TO THE CONVENTION OF 1933
speechtext: I had no intention at this point of discussing rates of duty on articles coming from France; I expected we should come to that later. I am simply making the point that wherever these reductions are made they should at least go to the people, and not lead to the establishment of what seems to be a contbine. Certain vested interests, certain monopolists, seem to have secured the privilege of dealing in these pharmaceutical preparations. As far as the general principle of a tax on luxuries is concerned I am in perfect agreement with the hon. member for Lincoln. I would go perhaps much further than he would in putting taxes on liquor.

maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE TRADE AGREEMENT   BILL TO CONFIRM ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL OF 1935 TO THE CONVENTION OF 1933

I cannot weigh the balance as between the producer of grapes in the Niagara peninsula and the producer of wheat in the prairie provinces. maintopic: CANADA-FRANCE TRADE AGREEMENT   BILL TO CONFIRM ADDITIONAL PROTOCOL OF 1935 TO THE CONVENTION OF 1933

Therefore, in order to preserve what we have in the way of a wheat market in France and to increase that market to the greatest extent possible, certain concessions have been made to France in this treaty. Mr. CAHiAJN: The right hon. gentleman will have to put that question to the acting Prime Minister, because I am not the official negotiator of treaties for the government. Listening to the minister, I have been most interested in learning of the difficulties which were encountered because of the United Kingdom-Canada agreements. I believe those difficulties bear out what hon. members on this side have been saying. Those Imperial conference agreements as drafted have stood in the way of the negotiations of agreements with other countries. It is quite clear that Australia has had to be consulted, Great Britain has had to be consulted and other parts of the empire have had to be consulted before the government could negotiate any trade agreement, even one as small as the one now under consideration. Coupling with that the fact that, within the past year, mo other trade agreements have been negotiated, it would clearly indicate' that the provisions of the United Kingdom-Canada agreements are presenting real difficulties. It is not long since we heard some talk about possible reciprocity in trade between Canada and the United States, but it now would look as though those negotiations too have fallen through. If they have, I have not the slightest doubt the greater part of the difficulty has been that of getting over the handicaps which the United Kingdom-Canada agreements have placed in the way of negotiations between this country and the United States. From the discussion we have had on this particular measure at least that much is clear.
One other point is apparent-in fact, quite as apparent this evening as it was from what we witnessed this afternoon-namely that as between themselves hon. gentlemen opposite are not much happier over their trade agreements than they are over their social legislation. It looks as though the function of the opposition, so far as opposing is concerned, or at least so far as discovering limitations is concerned, has to all intents and purposes been usurped by a large section of hon. gentlemen opposite.

I wish to make a few remarks in general in regard to pension matters. In the first place I commend the work of the acting chairman of the present pension commission. For the first time, I think, the returned men feel that they have a sympathetic hearer on the board, and when I use the word sympathetic I do not mean that a pension will be granted in every instance but I do mean that since the' present chairman came to the commission we have had patient and fair dealing in all these cases, whether a pension was granted or refused.
In discussing this matter I suggest that there are three presumptions in regard to pension cases which we must take into consideration. The first presumption is that there are a small minority in this country and even in this house who believe that the returned man has received too much, that he has been too well treated. The second presumption is that this country and this parliament have always been anxious to have generous treatment given the returned man. But there is a third presumption that, in spite of this general wish on the part of the people and the parliament of Canada, there has been a certain antagonism from the beginning of the pension organization up to the present time. I wish to discuss what I regard as the obstacles that were encountered from 1921 to 1923 and 1924. Those of us who were interested then in pension matters will remember that we had to deal with what I might call threats made by certain officials of the pension board. Those returned men who were getting a small pension received a threat during those years that unless they commuted their pension they

would have it reduced or eliminated altogether by the medical examiners and the pension representatives of that day. There are certain men who commuted their pension and who do not yet know that they can return to the pension status under certain conditions. A second obstacle was the poor assessment that was made, and even to this day there is no systematic way in which the pension is estimated and disability allowed. If the procedure of the insurance companies were followed instead of having these nineteen different percentages, then each case would be fairly decided. In those first years these two factors caused a good deal of disagreement and discontent and the result was that an appeal court was formed. That court functioned for a time, but as soon as it began to give decisions favourable to the returned men the pension board immediately sat upon it and arranged a procedure and adopted methods to be followed, and in consequence there was antagonism between the two boards.
Those of us who sat on the different committees in .those years will remember that bwing to the difference of opinion, that antagonism which existed between these two bodies, the returned men did not receive just and fair treatment. A strong demand was then made for changes and the Ralston commission was appointed. This brought to light a great many injustices and the result was the legislation of 1928. The proposals were brought to us in the committee by the legion and other interested societies and they were adopted. The hon. member for Red Deer and I were the only two opponents of that legislation. We pointed out that it was impracticable and would lead to greater confusion. We asked that the pension board should be increased and that travelling quorums should be appointed, and that the hearing of these cases should be in public. They proposed the appointment of tribunals; they proposed the appointment of pension advocates ; they proposed an appeal board. The result was that the legislation broke down absolutely and the sufferers were the returned men.
While this parliament and the people of Canada desire to have generous treatment given the returned men, there have been from the beginning certain obstacles that ha\ e prevented the men from receiving that treatment which it was intended they should get, and in consequence the 1928 board has been done away with. We proposed that the appeal court should be resorted to by the returned men, but what happened? Instead of

Supply-Pensions-European War
being used by the returned men it was usurped by the pension board, and every case decided favourably to the returned men was at once appealed, even before the decision was handed down. Some twenty-four or twenty-five thousand cases have been passed along, kicked around from one body to the other. Death has reduced the number to some extent, and men have gone down to their graves without that generous treatment which this country intended they should receive, and this because of procrastination, because of the impossibility of these boards functioning properly, so that a great deal of money has been misspent. If that money, instead of being wasted as it was in the years that have gone, had been given to the applicants this country would have been dollars ahead and these men would not have suffered as they have done.
Then we come to the 1931 legislation, and again an obstacle was put in the way. What has been the result of all this? Instead of a returned man receiving favourable, generous treatment, he has not been treated fairly. Clever young counsel were employed by the pension board against inexperienced pension advocates, and in nearly every one of the cases the returned man lost out. The only benefit that I can see from this legislation is that parliament has passed measures by which members of organizations have received remunerative positions while the returned men have practically lost out.
I come now to some other factors which have also worked against the returned men. They were up against it from 1921 to 1923; they were up against it again in the legislation of 1928 and 1931; but when we come to 1933- and I do not want anyone to think I am talking in a partisan way because these things have happened under both Liberal and Conservative governments-the result was murderous. In that year the men were cut off wholesale, their pensions being reduced or limited. How was this done? I want to bring these matters before the present chairman because I believe we have a sympathetic chairman of the commission and a sympathetic minister. In 1933, files away back in the years gone by were searched by somebody, and if certain statements could be found there, the man's pension was reduced or eliminated. I do not want to take up the time of the committee in discussing a great number of cases, but I shall give one that is significant. A man was pensioned for epilepsy. In 1933 a search of his file was made and it was found away back in the file that he had made a statement that he had a headache when he was a boy
eleven years old. It was held that his epilepsy commenced then. The man had never had a seizure. He was examined in Canada; he took his training in this country and reached England without any seizure whatever. Yet on that statement his pension was cut by forty per cent. I have searched his file. The man disputes this statement, but even if it is true that he did make the statement, it is contrary to the act that his pension should be cut down. I want to draw the attention of the committee, the general public and the returned men to section 11 which states:
No deduction shall be made from the degree of actual disability of any member of the forces who has served in a theatre of actual war on account of any disability or disabling condition which existed in him at the time at which he became a member of the forces.
I want now to discuss an even more marked case than that. In 1933 a man had his pension reduced because he was said to have had pneumonia prior to his enlistment. He had served two or three years in France. According to that section his pension could not be reduced, nevertheless it was reduced. I do not doubt glaring mistakes have been made, but these should not be charged up against just cases which come within the act.
The question of marriage cases has been dealt with and a decision will be given. Then we come to the question of the immorality cases. I wonder whether the committee and the general public remember the promise given that men would be generously treated, yet a case was brought before the board where a woman had her pension cut off in 1920 and it remained cut off for fourteen years simply because some jealous or other person made a statement against her character. That sort of thing has happened in five or six cases in my constituency and vicinity, although it is contrary to' the provision of the act which reads:
The pension of any female pensioner who is found to be a common prostitute or who openly lives with any man in the relationship of man and wife without being married to him shall be suspended, discontinued or cancelled.
Yet not one of those cases in which the pension has been out off on the ground of immorality comes within the terms of section 39. Someone goes into the woman pensioner's house and finds a man's coat there, and her pension is cut off. There were three children, but of course their pension was continued. In this case a pension was cut off for fourteen years from a woman whose husband was killed in France and who is left with three children. I do not know how the decision was reached, because it was contrary to the
