act. It must be proved, first, that the woman is a common prostitute, or second, that she is living as the wife of a man to whom she has not been married, and in not one of those cases were those conditions fulfilled. The returned men are awaiting the decision in the marriage case. I think it was a great interference to disturb a marriage that had been in existence for fifteen or sixteen years, putting a name upon the returned man's wife because she could not produce a certificate of her first husband's death which had occurred twenty years before.
The compassionate benefit of doubt clause has been practically ignored. I will agree that the department have treated cases in accordance with that clause, but the pension part of it has been absolutely ignored. I would like to draw the attention of the committee and of the returned men to four factors in the great war in which compassion and the benefit of the doubt should be given. The men who served one year in the war at the front saw a certain amount of hardship, but only those who served four years at the front can really describe what the men went through. There are four conditions I want to bring before the chairman and before the new minister. The first is the conditions on Salisbury plain. Anyone who lived through those conditions knows that eighty per cent, yes ninety per cent of the men came out of there with bronchitis, and they had not recovered from that when they were suddenly thrust into the gas attack in April. The pension experts tell us, following the United States decision, that any person who suffered from gas would not have tuberculosis or would not have a tendency to tuberculosis. In fact the United States decision was that it helped to cure a case tending to tuberculosis. But unfortunately their statistics are based upon experiences which followed the use of almost, one might say, perfect gas masks through which the men suffered very little and where they recovered. The Canadian statistics cannot be made up, because our men who went through that first gas attack endured it when there was no protection and are in ninety per cent of the cases lying in Flanders field, and those who survived and came home I contend are liable to any pulmonary trouble that you can name. After gas masks have been provided and protection is perfected, the statistics are very different as with figures for those who endured a gas attack without any protection or help.
Then I want to take the third case. Those who were in the Somme went through conditions that no people in this country know
I Mr. Ross.J
much about. The men who served the first year and came home did not have the experiences of men who served the second, third or fourth years. When men lay in mud in the Somme valley, as they did for eight days, came back and slept in the Albert mud fields and brick yards for a night or two, and then went back for their three days' rest only to return to the mud fields again, they went through an experience from which any disease might result. Then, fourth, was the Passchen-daele field. When we of the Canadian corps went into Passchendaele there was a record there that the force that preceded us did not get fifty per cent of their wounded out of that ground. I have walked on those duck-boards, and the men who went in by daylight could see those bodies that were almost as sleepers under the duck-boards. Any men who went through a month of that and could come back and be the men they were before would be supermen. They are liable to any form of breakdown of their system.
Now in deciding those cases, and having regard to the benefit of the doubt, I can say without hesitation that no man who went through either the first year on Salisbury plain, or the first gas attack, or the Somme experience, and lastly through Passchendaele, could do so without some effect on his system. In these cases I think some consideration should be given to the experience instead of trying to cut pensions down. And in future consideration of cases there should be nothing of the kind which I quote now. Here is a returned man who has had an operation. He has adhesions. He has had them for a year or two. What do you think of this record put on his medical sheet? This is given by one of the surgeons. Just following an operation you may have adhesions, medical men in this room will agree, but when these adhesions keep on for a year or two years I do not think it deserves such a report as this on the man's sheet:
Think this man with the greatest security can get out and do the hardest of labour without the slightest ill effect, and it will help the pain.
What chance has that man before any board, with that entered on his sheet, signed by the surgeon of the department? Statements supposed to have been made by a man preceding enlistment should be checked up with the greatest diligence. Here is a man who says:
On my sheet is the fact that I have had pneumonia, that I had arthritis, but I never was sick in my life before my enlistment.

Supply-Pensions-European War
If the statement is there it should be shown and proven, because I followed it in one case and I could not find anything to justify any such statement. It seems that these statements are passed down as one board follows another. They are simply copied from the previous record without ever going back of it. I think the pension board should study these things thoroughly. I will give you four or five cases. Here is one man noted as having had pneumonia in 1902, as having had rheumatic fever in 1911, and his pension is reduced forty per cent. The man says he never had them. Here is a case within my own knowledge. The man has tuberculosis to-day. He was run over in France by a gun limber loaded with live shells weighing one or two tons. He had served two years, and never had a sign of a cough or lung affection of any kind until he was run over by this gun limber. Then he is home with tuberculosis and they find that some time previous to his enlistment he had pneumonia. They reduce his pension in spite of the section that I read in which it is provided that any previous trouble should not be counted in the reduction of his disability. Here is another: they wrote to the man and said, "Before your case comes on we want a little bit more evidence." I have two or three letters which contain this phrase: "We want a little bit more evidence." What kind of evidence? The man's comrade is not believed; anyone connected with him is not believed. There is only one way he can get . it, and that is from the record of the hospital in which he was treated in France or in England; yet, when that is searched for, it cannot be found. That is where the man could get his evidence. If the records of these hospitals were produced they would show the medical men who attended him, and the nurses; but the man has to suffer because the record is lost. See how it works against a good -man. I have had this in hundreds of cases: A man who is at the front comes to us in the ambulance and says: "I don't want to go back." He has a temperature, and the regulations say that if he has a temperature for three days he must be evacuated. But this man says, "I don't want to go back." We put him in a rest station and try to treat him. He comes out recovered and goes back to the front; he comes back again and again, he goes to the front. The record is absolutely lost or destroyed, but every week a return is made from the ambulances of the men and their complaints. Yet they say: "Go and get a little further evidence."
Here is another case: they say, "Investigate carefully all records of the Calvin Company." But the Calvin Company is long out of business and most of those who were connected with it are dead. The captain of the boat on which the accident happened is dead. The man cannot possibly get the evidence, but the accident on the boat is the reason he cannot get his pension for another accident that happened in France.
I hope I have made this clear. I am saying it perhaps for the last time. I shall give a summary of these things, but first I want to read a letter. May I- say I saw this thing through from the beginning to the end, having been among the first in and the last out of France, and I did think that my medical experience there would be worth something. I received a copy of this letter:
It is with considerable diffidence that I write, but the situation is urgent and demands public support.
This is not written recently, but I want to show the house the situation.
Such action before now has compelled parliament to act. Brigadier General Ross has questioned in the house decision given against the tubercular and disabled soldiers in many instances by the pension board.
Parliament exhibits a curious apathy to the question.
No one in Canada is better qualified to give an expert opinion on this question than Brigadier General Ross

I shall not read any more of that or it might be said I read it for my own benefit But here is the thing:
During the war time Canada in a more or less hysterical manner stated the returned soldiers would be looked after and the service rendered would never be forgotten.
Has it been so? I say emphatically it has not so far as our sick are concerned. Listen to this:
If a man on his enlistment was passed as fit by the medical officers then this country cannot morally refuse assistance if tuberculosis has developed within a reasonable period after his discharge from the service.
The writer of this was not then on, the pension board, but he is a member of that board to-day and I have not seen any more generous treatment being given our returned men. Here is a case of which I have personal knowledge. In the battle of Loos we had about seven hundred gas cases. Due to the fact that our treatment had been prepared we evacuated from the front line only twenty-six of the seven hundred, and this man was one of the twenty-six. Hon. members will agree that this man would not be expected to improve as the years went by; I know that

Supply-Pensions-European War
to-day he is in a chronic condition, but here is his experience with the pension board. In 1923 he obtained a pension of fifteen per cent, which continued until 1926, when it was increased to twenty-five per cent. In 1927 it was increased again to forty per cent and in 1928 to fifty per cent, where it remained until 1933. To-day that man is an absolute wreck, but in 1933 his pension was reduced to thirty per cent. Can that be justified? Can any reason be given for such action? His pension was gradually increased to fifty per cent, but in 1933 it was reduced to thirty per cent though to-day he is thirty per cent worse than he has been at any time since coming home.
I think I have given enough illustrations, and I should like to make certain proposals in this regard. I think the time has come when these permanent medical officers should be exchanged. These officers have given opinions; very often a man has had a decision given against him. He comes up for a rehearing against the same officer, and these officers are not big enough to change their opinions even though the condition may be progressing. So I think the time has come when these permanent officers should be moved. Let them be sent to some other stations; let the men from those other stations exchange with them. It is impossible to get these men to change their opinions no matter how bad the cases may be. Then again I think we have been just a little too ready to take these ex-service men from the eligible pension list and put them under the veterans' allowance. I think they deserve a little better treatment than that. I have mentioned four factors, and I think it will be agreed that any man who has been affected by one, two, three or all four is to-day in such a condition that age should not be counted. I would wipe out the age limit in regard to those returned men; I would make them total disability cases whether they were forty, fifty or sixty years of age. How can anything be determined by the age of the man? In 1923 I heard the then minister of pensions say, "We have reached the peak, and in about two years these pensions will begin to decrease." Why, we have not reached the peak yet; so long as there are any of these men left they are going to suffer from their experiences.
Let me say openly that I cannot understand why the chief medical adviser of the department is also a commissioner. Is it reasonable that a man who has given a decision should sit as a member of the board reviewing that decision? The thing is ridiculous; the chief medical adviser should not
fMr. Ross.]
be a commissioner. Perhaps I should be a little more lenient, Mr. Chairman, but if you had spent four years with these men and had seen how they suffered-and you must remember that some of them did not know what suffering was until they returned home -you would feel as I do. I may not appeal to the house again for fair treatment of these men, but I hope my experience has been worth something to them. I have refused to take any job, because I believe it my duty, after I have seen them go through so much, to back them up in their demand for the fair and generous treatment they were promised.

I have no desire to
delay these estimates, Mr. Chairman, but to a certain extent I must endorse what the hon. member for Kingston City has said as to the unrest among the returned men and what they think of the treatment they have received in the past. I have been fortunate enough to have been on every pension committee appointed since the war, I think, and we have always done the best we could, but sometimes, as the hon. member has pointed out, the best does not seem to be any too good.
In the early days following the war pensions were very readily granted and the greatest trouble of hon. members of the house was that it was thrown up to them that 'George Jones and Dick Smith had pensions which they did not deserve. That was the main complaint in those days. As time passed and the memories of the war faded, however, the contrary became the case. For many years we had at the head of the pensions board a man who was almost universally disliked by the returned soldiers. He was a gentleman of whose personal integrity I have nothing to say; undoubtedly he was an honourable gentleman, but he was said to stand so upright that he was in danger of falling over and injuring the back of his neck. He does not occupy that position now.
Another complaint has been voiced by the hon. member for Kingston City, and it has been a prominent complaint on the part of returned men's organizations for some years. It is that our chief medical officer was not likely to change his opinion in favour of an applicant for pension. I feel as my hon. friend feels that the appointment of the chief medical officer as a member of the commission perhaps was not a very wise move. We all know that cases have arisen from time to time in which the decisions of the board have been entirely contrary to the purpose of the act. Section 11 of the Pension Act distinctly states that a man who went to France apparently physically fit and who saw

Supply-Pensions-European War
service in an active theatre of war should have no charge made against him with regard to his eligibility for pension. That is to say, any disease that he might have had before enlistment should not couint against him unless-and I think the hon. member for Kingston City forgot this exception-it was a case of misrepresentation or deliberate fraud. I have known men who went overseas after passing not one but perhaps two or three examinations in Canada; they passed further examinations in England and did their duty in France, and yet because a man had measles when he was only two years old he is stated to be ineligible for pension, or if in fact he is getting a pension it is reduced. One instance in particular appealed to me. I have in mind a man whom I know well and who at1 present is totally blind. He saw service in France, and has been in hospitals in Canada. He applied for a pension. The statement was made that he responded to a Wassermann test-hon. members know what that means-and that his disability was a result of venereal disease. He has taken an affidavit that he never had any disease of that kind, nor did his people so far as he knows. I believe the man is honest. He was told that if he said he had the disease he would receive a pension for aggravation, but when he says he has not he cannot get the pension. I believe there are many cases similar to the one I have described which should have the sympathetic consideration of the commission. Perhaps in this house and throughout the country there is an element who think enough has been done for the returned soldier, but I am quite sure they form only a negligible portion of our population. I believe the people desire that every returned man who is eligible for pension shall have at least that compensation to which by law he is justly entitled.

To a great extent I concur in the observations of the hon. members for Kingston City and Parry Sound. I was under the impression that before the last amendments to the Pension Act were made one of the great stumbling blocks in connection with giving justice to ex-service men was the fact that the onus was on him to prove that his disability was due to war service. It was impossible to present that proof. I would say, not in any spirit of criticism- and I want the minister thoroughly to understand that-that in the many cases with which I have been connected I have not
known of one in which the ex-service man received the benefit of the doubt when consideration had been given to the question whether his disability had been due to war service. So long as that condition prevails justice cannot be given to ex-service men.
I believe a great deal of the difficulty now experienced by ex-service men applying for pensions is due to what happened in the days immediately following the war when the men were returning to Canada. Every soldier was tired of war and anxious to get back into civil life. That is where a great deal of the difficulty originated. Thousands and thousands of young Canadians returned from France and were discharged without any examination. To a great extent the fault was that of the soldier, because he wanted to get away from the army and back into civil life. Perhaps in many cases soldiers did not wish to admit there was anything physically wrong with them, and for that reason examinations did not amount to anything. In the years which followed, however, disabilities appeared in some of the soldiers who had been discharged. The statement was then made, "Well, when this man was discharged he was physically fit and his file did not show any disability." I believe to a great extent that is the difficulty with which we have to contend to-day. The hon. member for Kingston City made some observations regarding medical sheets and files. I know many applications have been turned down because the files did not show the applicant had been in a hospital or even that he had .been wounded or gassed. I have always contended that those refusals were ridiculous, because files were lost overseas. There was a war on, and in many cases no records were kept where men had been gassed or wounded. After a lapse of five or ten years, these men having since come back to civil life, nothing can be found on their files. That is the difficulty, and because of it I submit that in every case the returned man should receive the benefit of the doubt. He does not receive that benefit to-day, and in this observation I am not criticizing the pension commission. Perhaps they are more or less confined within the four corners of the act, but there should be more flexibility in its application; the humanitarian view should be taken. Speaking broadly I believe the Dominion of Canada has treated her ex-service men as well as has any country which participated in the great war. That however is no reason why injustices and weaknesses in the act should not be remedied and the proper amendments made. I fully expected that amendments would be brought

Supply-Pensions-European War
down during the present session, and I regret the minister and the government have not seen fit to do so. I hope that at the next session of parliament, no matter what party is returned to power, amendments to the Pension Act may be made. I have no desire to delay the minister's estimates. I could mention four or five cases which have come under my observation within the last few months but I shall not take the time of the committee any more than to emphasize this point, that soldiers discharged at the end of the war showing no disability have found difficulty in proving their cases.
Since the depression, if we choose so to describe it, a condition which has been worldwide in its scope, when thousands of men have been out of work, ex-service men receiving or not receiving pensions who are unemployed and depending more or less on charity find their condition of disability aggravated. The suggestion to reduce the pension of an unemployed soldier is in my mind quite wrong. The hon. member for Kingston spoke about this matter. Undoubtedly the state of mind of a man who is unemployed, especially if he has a family dependent upon him, will aggravate a disability. Such cases should receive the sympathetic consideration of the pension board. This country spends considerable money for pensions. There are some people, not very many I am glad to say, who think that perhaps the ex-service men have received all the consideration they should receive. I agree with the hon. member for Kingston City who has reminded the committee that when the war was on those who enlisted to go overseas were promised definitely that if they were spared to come back they would be taken care of, if they were disabled they would be pensioned and if they were killed their families would be taken care of. I think it is the duty of this parliament to see that the promises which were made to the men who enlisted in the great war are carried out to the very letter.

I assume that every hon. member receives a great number of complaints from returned men as to the manner in which the Pension Act is administered. I come from a constituency in which there is a large number of returned men but I must confess that I have not followed the administration of this act very closely. As far as the business of the house is concerned, my colleague the hon. member for Red Deer represents us in this corner in connection with pension matters. We have turned over to him a great many cases and have left it to him to work out the details of the amendments

which might be brought before the house. I should like to associate myself with the hon. member for Kingston City in urging that the returned man be given the benefit of the doubt and granted not only fair but generous treatment.

Anything I may say in regard to this matter will be said simply as a civilian doctor, I not having had any military experience. The state of affairs to which the hon. member for Kingston City has directed attention undoubtedly is a blot upon the social life of this country which probably will not be erased until the last overseas casualty has passed on. One of the things which has caused much unhappiness and dissatisfaction among the returned men is the fact that a great many men in rather good circumstances are receiving extensive pensions from the government which they probably do not need. Another phase of the matter is the fact that many men were invalids before they entered the army. It is true that these men were aocepted by the examining boards, but they never did one day's service. I have met a number of such cases and undoubtedly they create dissatisfaction and unhappiness among the bona fide men, many of whom are wrecks to-day. I have in mind one old fellow whom I attended for many years prior to the war. This man has had bronchitis all the days of his life. He was accepted and went to Great Britain where he continued to have bronchitis. He came back to Canada and has been in the hospital on and off ever since. His overseas service has nothing whatever to do with his bronchitis. I have personal knowledge of other cases where men are receiving substantial pensions for overseas service when in fact they are just as healthy as I am. On the other hand, men who died in misery and agony, undoubtedly the victims of overseas service, had been unable to obtain a five cent piece by way of pension. It is not always easy to say whether or not a man's condition is the result of overseas service, but if a man has risked his life for his government and his fellow citizens, it seems to me that the least a government can do is to give him medical assistance and treatment as long as he lives, whether or not his illness may have been caused by overseas service.
The hon. member for Kingston City has referred to the staff of medical men. I think it would be a mighty good plan to do away with these men because they are such a hard-boiled bunch. Once it is decided that a man is not sick, in their eyes he can never be sick again. I think the best thing the

Supply-Pensions-European War
government could do would be to get rid of these permanent medical men and rely upon the ordinary medical practitioners to give the returned men the justice which they deserve. Any medical man who has any sensibility is disgusted with the way these things are handled. Many men appeal to us who are simply wrecks, and whether or not their condition is due to overseas service, it is the duty of this country to make some reparation for the disabilities they suffer as a result of the service which they have given to the Canadian people.
Have the marriage cases been discussed as yet?

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: No.

Could the minister make a statement with reference to the situation now prevailing in connection with the marriage cases which were discussed in the committee on February 13 of last year? I should like to know the number disposed of and the number yet to be disposed of.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
Before answering that question let me say that I appreciate the discussion on this subject which has been led by the hon. member for Kingston city. I have no doubt that many hon. members do not know the magnificent record of the hon. member. He was in charge of the entire medical arrangements of the Canadian corps and was responsible for the evacuation of the wounded. Wherever returned men gather they recognize the work he did and the great sympathy he has for them at the present time. One point which he brought out impressed me, as I am sure it impressed any hon. member who has first hand information. The hon. member referred to the conditions which prevailed at Salisbury plain in 1914 and 1915, at Ypres at the time of the gas attack and at the Somme. I cannot speak personally of the conditions at Passchendaele, but I have heard that they were just as bad or perhaps worse. Any man who faced the conditions at Salisbury or the other places in my opinion would not be in the same condition of health as when he went in, even though he did not receive an actual wound. It is not the ones with actual wounds that give difficulty, because there is not much trouble with respect to a man who has an arm or a leg off; it is the cases referred to, men who have possibly got along fairly well but who suffer from the strain and stress of life. I am confident that this is so, and I think that more and more of these cases will come to the fore and will have to be dealt with as sympathetically as possible.
I noted what the hon. member for Kingston City said with regard to the loss of records. That undoubtedly is a point that comes up frequently in the search for the medical history of some of the men. He also said-and others have voiced the sentiment-that sympathy has been in evidence since Mr. Justice Taylor took over the chairmanship of the board. I express my acquiescence in that view. Since I have been in charge of the department I have had repeated instances of the personal interest and sympathy which Mr. Justice Taylor has in these cases. I have had a very wide experience with pensioners in my practice of medicine, and I have never yet seen a man with a pension who I thought should not have it. You will see in the papers and you will hear from time to time that so and so has a pension which he does not deserve any more than someone else, and yet in a number of these cases in which I have been the medical attendant I know that the men have had serious troubles, deepseated, underlying and not evident to anyone passing them on the street. They were in receipt of pensions, and so long as they were quiet they got along well and looked well. But they could not have stood hard work; they would have gone down hill and died. Sometimes people are rather thoughtless in their attitude to those receiving pensions. My personal observation has been as I have stated; I have never seen anyone getting a pension who I thought should not have it. I think that as a general rule things are going along much better under Mr. Justice Taylor.
I have made notes of the suggestions put forward by hon. members and they will certainly be given every consideration. With regard to the marriage cases I do not know that I can do better than read, although it is rather long, a statement given me by the chairman of the pensions commission with regard to them:
With reference to the number of eases which have been dealt with where the validity of the pensioner's marriage has been questioned, I beg to submit the following figures. These figures only include the cases which have actually reached the pay branch to date, and might be supplemented, perhaps, by fifteen or twenty other eases which have been dealt with, but have not actually reached the pay branch. In all 632 cases have arisen which might be classified as follows:-
(1)	Granted: 160.
In these cases the commission have acknowledged the validity for pension purposes of the marriage in question, and the pensioner has been so advised.
This item would include a number of cases where the commission has obtained, or been supplied with, additional information which has cleared up the problem.

Supply-Pensions-European War
(2)	Not Granted: 98.
These are cases in which either by the admission of the parties themselves, or by material already on the pensioner's file, or after a hearing before two commissioners, it has been decided that the marriage cannot be recognized as sufficient for pension purposes.
These include cases where pensioner has admitted that he never went through a marriage ceremony; cases wdiere former spouses of one of the parties have been located, and ascertained to be living at the time of the marriage to the pensioner, without any action having been taken to dissolve the previous marriage; cases in which the time has been very short between the separation from the first spouse and the contracting of the second marriage, and in which it would be impossible for any presumption of death to arise; and an odd case in which the pensioner has asked us not to make further investigation. Other cases might be included in this number, but the ones I have mentioned are the principal ones.
(3)	Investigating: 81.
These are cases in which we have asked the pensioner to submit further evidence; or to put in the form of a statutory declaration statements which may only have been made to us by letter, or in which we, ourselves, are trying to get the necessary information apart from the pensioner. I think every assistance is being afforded pensioners in this class of case; and the commission is even going to some expense in a number of cases, in order to assist the pensioner to get the necessary information. In addition, pensioner is being notified in each case that the district pensions advocate in his district will give him every assistance possible in the way of supplying any further information that may be required.
(4)	Awaiting Opportunity to Appear before the Commission: 54.
Some of these are cases in which we think the marriage of the pensioner cannot be recognized for pension purposes, but before cancelling the additional pension for his wife, we have given him an opportunity of appearing before the commission. Unless the facts are apparent from the file itself, or from the admission of the pensioner or his wife, we are not actually cancelling any additional pensions w-ithout first giving the pensioner an opportunity of appearing before the commission. In most cases of this kind, the additional pension is being continued until after he has a hearing. In a few cases, where the upholding of the marriage seems to be next to impossible, we have, in the meantime, suspended the nayment of additiona pension until the hearing.
Other cases which might be included in this class are those where we think, perhaps, the pensioner can best substantiate his marriage problem by attending, and giving evidence, before commissioners, instead of supplying affidavits. A number of hearings have been ordered in such cases, because the commission through it would' give the pensioner a better chance of retaining his additional pension for his wife; and also in cases where we had to consider the question of recovery of payments already made, and we wanted to inquire into the good or bad faith of the pensioner in
lMr. Sutherland.]
procuring payment of additional pension for a wife; or as to whether he was guilty of any fraud or deceit.
(5)	No Decisions Rendered: 239.
This number includes approximately 115 or 125 divorce problems where the validity of the pensioners' marriage depends upon the validity of a divorce obtained in the United States. These cases will probably all be settled by two or three general decisions. In many cases the circumstances are identical, but I have not yet given them final consideration; in other words, they were left to the last. They will be considered as a class as soon as the other cases are reasonably disposed' of.
The balance of the cases in which no decision has been rendered are cases which have not yet been reviewed and written up for my consideration. Mr. Wilson, departmental solicitor, is working continually on these cases, and it will not be long until they are all disposed of.
In nearly all of the eases where it has been found necessary to discontinue additional pension for wife, we have not cut off the additional pension for children, but continued to pay it under section 22 (4).
Generally speaking, the commission has adopted a principle that we will not recover moneys overpaid in connection with these marriage cases unless we decide that the overpayment was caused through fraud or deceit on the part of the pensioner. Fortunately, the number of cases w-here there has been fraud or deceit is not large.
New cases are arising from time to time which contain marriage problems, which the commissioners in the board room have thought it necessary to refer to me. Since the 1st of August, last, 250 cases, approximately, have been so referred, in addition to the number which were awaiting consideration upon my arrival. I think I might safely say that another six weeks or two months should see the marriage problem pretty well out of the way, except for cases that may be awaiting hearings before commissioners; and the cases which are arising from week to week.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext: There will be a supplementary item for 1934-35 on which I suggest any discussion might take place.

I would like to say
one further word on this matter, because what I had in mind has been pretty fully expressed by other hon. members who have spoken, particularly by the hon. member for Kingston City.
In common with, I suppose, every other hon. member, and especially with those who like myself have been associated with this

Supply-Pensions-European War
work for a number of years, I have had brought to my attention a great many individual cases in which pensions have been refused or reduced and the applicants have felt themselves aggrieved. I shall not bring any of these cases before the committee at this time, for I believe no good purpose could be served by my doing so, but I must say that in a number of these cases I found myself utterly at a loss to understand the action which brought about this situation. It seems to me that ordinary common sense, let alone ordinary humanity, would have dictated a different and more generous policy.
As I conceive the matter, the great problem lies in this, that perhaps above all other laws the success of this one depends upon its administration. You cannot legislate to meet individual cases, and in almost every instance the plight of a particular applicant will depend almost wholly upon the discretion of the pension commission or those who serve imder and act for it. That is inevitable, because it is a law which above all others deals with humanity and naturally suffering humanity, varying in kind, in degree, and every case must be dealt with on its merits. This is what makes it so peculiarly important that the administration should be carried on by those who not only are intelligent and fully conversant with the subject, but have a really sympathetic and understanding attitude. That becomes more and more imperative as the years go by, because more and more it is becoming impossible for any new applicant to bring forward definite and convincing evidence, and the common sense of the commission must be exercised in deciding whether, in view of all the circumstances, the overwhelming probability must be that the application is worthy of consideration. It seems to me that we are faced again with the fact, that the most deserving cases are always the most difficult to prove. The man who from the beginning has made application or has camped on the doorstep of the department every time he has had an ache, is the one who can be taken care of; but the man who above all others deserves consideration, the man who without making application has done his best to carry on under his own steam despite disability, until the crushing weight of that disability and of increasing years makes it impossible for him to do so, finds through his own meritorious action that there is a gap of evidence which makes the proof of continuity almost impossible. I believe in those cases above all others the administrative bodies, the commission and those
serving it, should temper their justice with a good deal of discretional humanity.
There is just one other point I would like to make, and it is by way of support of a suggestion made by the hon. member for Kingston City, who knows whereof he speaks, namely that the medical officers at the various points should be changed around from time to time. In common with many others I have had cases come before me from time to time where men applied for a reboarding, and I must say that usually a reboarding has been granted. But when the reboarding takes place before the same medical examiners who made the former examination, human nature as it has been exemplified in many of these cases is such that there is almost an overwhelming disinclination on the part of the examiners to admit that they might possibly have been mistaken the last time. It seems to me that it would be all to the good from the standpoint of justice and of getting a fresh viewpoint, a fresh angle, a fresh application of medical skill, if the reboarding could take place under some medical officer who had had no former connection with the case, who would consider it without bias and have no former decision to hamper his present consideration. I believe such a move would go far towards bringing about justice in some cases and removing dissatisfaction in many more. Where I have had cases reboarded perhaps three or four times, the third or fourth time the men appeared before the medical examiner the first remark made was this: "Oh, you are back here again, are you? What do you want now?" Well, it is impossible for any man to get a satisfactory examination when that is the attitude of the examining officers even before the examination begins; the man might just as well stay at home. I shall not go so far as to suggest, as was mentioned by someone, that we should scrap the whole examining body and put in fresh men on the ground that although they may have benefited by years of experience, there has occurred a hardening of the mental arteries which later renders them useless. But I would suggest, from my experience as a result of any obesrvations I have been able to make, that in the case of reboarding, in the case of a second or third or fourth examination of the same man, he should have the benefit of at least a change of physician, a change of attitude, an examination by a medical officer who, coming fresh to the consideration of that particular case, would be

Supply-Pensions-European War
unhampered by any previous decision on the same man or any preconceived opinion arising therefrom.
Before I close, I must in justice 6ay this- and it has been one of the most pleasurable parts of pension work during the last months -that the men appreciate the changing attitude of the administration during the past months and under the present chairman. I received just the other day a letter from the legion bodies in my part of the country, with whom I have had a certain amount of contact for a good many years, and for the first time they did not ask for anything and made no complaints. They wrote to inform me that the situation and the feeling had materially improved, almost to paraphrase the words of the hon. member for Kingston City -and they used almost the same expression- not so much that there had been many increases in pension, not so much that a few of the applications formerly refused are now receiving consideration, but because of the manner in which the applications are being received. Instead of simply a curt note, "application refused," they receive a courteous notice informing them not only that it has been refused but why it has been refused, in many cases convincing them that the application had not the merit which they thought it had, and in others giving the reason and the meaning behind the evidence which had made proper consideration impossible, thus giving them a reasonable chance to strengthen their case and bring forward the evidence necessary to making it complete. I wish to pay that tribute to a gentleman whom I have never met, the present chairman, but with whose work I have had some contact, as well as having some knowledge of the attitude of the returned men in my part of the country at least in relation to the present administration. They do not think it is perfect, but they do believe it is steadily improving. With increasing experience and its application in new administrative methods- and possibly with some amendments that may be necessary, although at the moment I know of none; I think administration is the important thing now-with that experience sympathetically applied I believe we shall be able finally to close for all time what has been a rankling grievance on the part of a section of our citizenship who I think above all others should be considered. I certainly hope so. I can say this perhaps with the greater freedom and force because I am not a returned man, but have had contact with the returned men and have to some extent had their confidence. I believe that should be our attitude not merely on sentimental

grounds but on the grounds stated so forcibly by the hon. member for Kingston City, having regard to the fact that the experience through which they have gone in many cases must have burnt out their power of resistance and left them a prey to disease and premature old age. We hope that with this sympathetic and understanding administration we shall be able to meet the situation more fully than ever before to the end that that rankling sense of injustice may be removed.

Empire settlement scheme, including grants authorized by the governor in council, $34,250.
What is the increase in this vote for?

speakeroldname: Hon. W. A. GORDON (Acting Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: This has to do with the empire settlement scheme agreement, entered into I think in 1926 or 1927 between the British government and ourselves, whereby young British lads were brought to Canada. Under the terms of the agreement, within a period of time which brought them to the age of twenty-five, I think, they were entitled upon having saved $500 to obtain a loan from the dominion government of $1,000, from the province of $250, and from the British government of $1,250, making in all $2,500. Several young chaps are entitled to these loans; some of them were entitled some three years ago. I have seen a number of them and have urged upon them that they would be well advised not to start to take on obligations. A person having saved $500 in farm work is doing pretty well. Up to the present we have not had to advance money to any of these boys, but enough of them are entitled under the agreement to take advantage of the loan if they persist and it would come to the amount asked for. I am hopeful, however, that none of them will undertake such obligations, because I know what it means.
Is that the reason for the increase in the vote?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Yes, that is the reason.

Supply-Immigration-Soldier Settlement

There is a matter I wish to take up with the minister under this item. It is in connection with an order in council, I believe it was, passed about 1933, under which soldier settlers who paid a certain amount of money were given credit for an additional amount, I believe double the amount they paid.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: That was by statute.

I have
had it brought to my attention several times, both by letter and by interviews with returned men, particularly in the dried out areas, that the men have not been able to pay anything in recent years because they have not had any crop. They want to know how they stand in regard to that provision in case they have a crop this year-whether they will get the same credit. In other words men who have a crop and are paying something get a credit on their loan, whereas those who have no crop are not getting any benefit whatever. What will their position be under that legislation in case they are able to pay something in the future?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It was not by order in council but by legislation. Under that legislation if they get a crop and are able to pay something this year they will get credit dollar for dollar on the amount paid in.

During the legion convention held here I think last year a resolution was passed asking that where a returned soldier say in any of the western provinces, who already had some farm land acquired other land through the soldier settlement board, which took security on all his land, including that of which he was in possession before he went to the war, this previously owned land should be freed from encumbrance because of any indebtedness to the government through the settlement scheme. Has the government given any consideration to that?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The resolution to which the hon. member referred has not come pointedly to my attention, although it has been under review by offiecrs of the department. I shall be glad to make myself more familiar with the resolution, and if it appears that there is hardship by reason of the attitude of the board, and it is possible to correct it without statutory amendment, I shall be very glad to take such action as seems proper.

The answer of the minister is indefinite. It is remarkable if .the resolution has not been forwarded to him;
it is more remarkable that, if it has, the minister is not more conversant with it. It seems to me that some legislative action should be taken to relieve this situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: It may seem strange, Mr. Chairman, but I have not had the resolution under my review. I know that I went through many of the resolutions passed last year with the representatives of the soldier organizations, but at the moment I cannot remember having dealt with the resolution to which the hon. gentleman has referred.

I have a copy in my
office. I did not anticipate that these estimates would be on to-night or I would have had it here.

The other day I
directed the attention of the minister to a condition existing in northern Saskatchewan in connection with these British settlers. I should like to ask the minister, if he has the information there, how many British families were settled under this scheme, how many are still in Canada, how many have asked for deportation and how many have been deported.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: As at December 31, 1934, the number of active settlers under the British family scheme, with loans, totalled 1,825. There were four families who had repaid their loans in cash and eleven families who had repaid their loans by sale agreements, that is, tripartite agreements. There were 1,323 families who had withdrawn from 3,000 family scheme after contracting loans; 180 families who had withdrawn from the scheme before contracting loans-that is, they never really got started-and three families who did not receive loans at all. Of the total number that came out under the scheme 135 families were deported. I do not use that word "deported" as the term is usually accepted; they just did not fit in and asked to be returned to Great Britain.

Has the minister the
information as to how many asked for deportation that were not deported?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
I am afraid I have not
the exact figures in that regard. I can say this, however, and I think I carry the percentages correctly in my mind. With respect to all people who were returned to Great Britain since August, 1930-and I do not refer only to this scheme; I include all Britishers-92 per cent first became deportable and then requested the department to return them to Great Britain. The other eight per cent were returned under orders of deportation. It has not been the policy of the department to be influenced too readily by pressure brought to bear for the return to 'Great Britain of Britishers who came to this country before 1930. At times some are prone to ask for return to the old land, and upon investigation it is found such people could get along if they tried. We do not encourage anything of that kind. The department does not like to see them return because while in some respects it may be true Great Britain offers more in the way of social insurance, or it may be that men wish to get back to their friends, yet we take the stand those men should have thought about such matters before they came here. I discourage action being taken because I harbour the view that this country presents great opportunities for anyone who wishes to take advantage of them, despite the fact that we hear it painted in rather gloomy colours.

May I again refer to
the people in northern Saskatchewan about whom I spoke the other day. They were brought in under the three thousand family scheme. It is unfortunate that most of those people were put on abandoned soldier settlement lands, and they never had a chance from the beginning. They have utterly failed, they are now destitute, and the information I receive is that their application for deportation has been refused. When this scheme was first suggested I pointed out the danger that these settlers coming into the country had not a ten per cent chance if they were placed on deserted soldier settlement lands, lands upon which the soldiers had not succeeded. I bring the matter to the attention of the minister because I have learned these people have asked for deportation. They cannot possibly make good, and I should like to know if it is a fact that deportation has been refused.

Privilege-Mr. Sauve

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: The departmental officials in the locality in which these settlers lived have made investigations. The hon. member is not quite right when he states that they- I believe they are about a half dozen in number-have not made any payments. My information is that one of them paid something over SI,100. The fact that they were settled on reverted soldier settlement lands does not by any means indicate that those lands could not support families.
They could not support immigrants.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: In any scheme, whether it be one affecting returned soldiers, a three thousand family scheme or any other land settlement scheme there is bound to be a considerable percentage of failures. The families who came to the western office, and to which reference was made in the house a few days ago, asked to be deported. Even if they had a proper case for deportation they are beyond reach of such action. I am told the British family scheme originated in 1924 and 1925, and they have been in this country more than five years. There is no fund upon which I could draw for purposes of returning them to Great Britain, even if it were desirable to do so. Of course there is no law which would justify my taking the action they suggest. I am not at all alarmed, because if we get fair climatic conditions in the coming season those people will take heart again.

Is the
interest paid under the original soldier settlement scheme still standing at the rate of six per cent?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext: Five per cent.

I should like again to refer to some circumstances I mentioned previously. I believe it is unfair to expect the returned soldiers in the dried out areas to be content to have this back interest charged against them, while the man who was fortunate enough to have a crop in the better districts got some relief by way of cancellation of half his interest, in the event of his paying the other half. It seems unfair to charge the interest against these men who have not had crops for the last two or three years.

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Labour; Minister of Mines
speechtext:
They will come under the Farmers' Creditors Arrangement Act.
Mr. McKENZIE Assiniboia): I do not think that will be satisfactory. In my view the government should consider doing something for these men by way of cancellation of a portion of the interest.
